alt: Three causes point to Japanese expansion from September 1931: nationalism and militarism, including officers' violence such as Inukai's assassination in 1932 and the February 26 Incident of 1936; Depression pressures, with the silk trade devastated and Manchuria offering resources; and instability in China under Chiang Kai-shek.
caption: Ideology, economics and opportunity combined; questions ask you to weigh them.

alt: Paired rows from 1931 to December 1941, actions on the left and responses on the right. Manchuria in 1931 and Manchukuo in 1932 met the Lytton Report and Japan's exit from the League without sanctions; pressure on north China met the Xi'an Incident and the United Front; war with China from 1937; the Tripartite Pact and Indochina met US economic pressure, ending in the oil embargo of 1941 and the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941.
caption: The League condemned but did not act; US pressure came late and helped trigger war.

after: ## Case study 2: German and Italian expansion, 1933-1940
alt: A grid comparing Germany and Italy. Ideology: Nazism sought to reverse Versailles, unite German-speakers and gain Lebensraum; Fascism celebrated war and imagined a new Roman empire. Economics: German rearmament strained the economy; Mussolini hoped colonies would distract from weakness. Below, the international system gave both openings: weakened collective security, hesitant Britain and France, a distrusted USSR and an absent US.
caption: Aggressors' aims and a weak international system together made expansion possible.

after: ## Case study 2: German and Italian expansion, 1933-1940
alt: Paired rows from 1935 to 1940, aggression on the left and responses on the right: German conscription against the Stresa Front, the invasion of Abyssinia against limited League sanctions and the Hoare-Laval plan, the Rhineland in 1936, the Anschluss and Munich in 1938, the occupation of Prague against the guarantee to Poland, the invasion of Poland and the declaration of war in 1939, and the fall of France and Italy's entry in 1940.
caption: Weigh the aggressors' intentions against the failure of responses, and how they interacted.

after: ## Worked example: reading a cartoon for Question 1(b)
alt: Two rows link a detail of an imagined 1935 cartoon to its meaning. A large, armed figure striding towards Abyssinia shows Mussolini was confident and determined to invade; a sleeping figure labelled League of Nations shows the League was too weak or unwilling to stop him. Each point earns one mark. Below: describing details without meaning earns little, and own knowledge is not needed.
caption: Two marks: two points about the message, each drawn from a detail.

alt: Two spectrums. Hitler's aims: A. J. P. Taylor (1961) saw an opportunist exploiting others' mistakes; Hugh Trevor-Roper saw long-held aims set out in Mein Kampf. Appeasement: Guilty Men (1940) blamed Chamberlain and his colleagues; later historians stressed military, economic and public-opinion constraints. A note asks how far Japanese expansion was planned in Tokyo or forced by commanders in the field.
caption: Plan or opportunism, blame or constraint: place each view, then judge.
